title: Historian Timothy Snyder Teaches a Free Course on Hitler, Stalin & How “It” Can Happen Here

When the his­to­ri­an Tim­o­thy Sny­der left Yale for the Uni­ver­si­ty of Toron­to in 20
body:
in History |   	September 9th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
When the his­to­ri­an Tim­o­thy Sny­der left Yale for the Uni­ver­si­ty of Toron­to in 2024, he took with him the prac­tice of occa­sion­al­ly putting his course lec­tures online, mak­ing them avail­able to any­one who cares to learn from them. Above, you can watch ten lec­tures from his recent course Hitler and Stal­in Today. In this course:
Sny­der exam­ines the Nazi and Sovi­et respons­es to the new glob­al­ized world they shared. The course begins with the colo­nial back­ground that made total­i­tar­i­an­ism pos­si­ble, and which remains an essen­tial ele­ment of our pol­i­tics now. Their ide­olo­gies are described as world­views and as prac­ti­cal pol­i­tics, with an empha­sis on the rea­sons for their appeal. Atten­tion to their poli­cies of mass killing, essen­tial events of twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry his­to­ry, instruct us about how “it” can hap­pen here. The study of dis­si­dent thought helps us to see con­nec­tions between his­tor­i­cal predica­ments and our own, and instructs us about pos­si­ble reac­tions as indi­vid­u­als and as cit­i­zens. The course asks what we have learned from the twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry and what lessons we should car­ry for­ward.
This course is for “any­one inter­est­ed in under­stand­ing the rela­tion­ship between his­to­ry and con­tem­po­rary democ­ra­cy.” You can stream the lec­tures above, or watch them on YouTube.
Hitler and Stal­in Today will be added to our col­lec­tion, 1,700 Free Online Cours­es from Top Uni­ver­si­ties.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Secret Career as a Japanese Art Dealer & How It Shaped His Architecture
description: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had some­thing in com­mon with Vin­cent van Gogh, who passed most of his much
body:
Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had some­thing in com­mon with Vin­cent van Gogh, who passed most of his much short­er life in more dire cir­cum­stances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pin­na­cle of the Amer­i­can archi­tec­tur­al pro­fes­sion, van Gogh remained prac­ti­cal­ly unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encoun­tered one anoth­er in the after­life, they’ve cer­tain­ly dis­cussed one sub­ject above all oth­ers: their shared appre­ci­a­tion for Japan­ese wood­block prints. Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured the col­lec­tion of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japan­ese art deal­ers and Amer­i­can tax col­lec­tors.
We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age hav­ing not evi­dent­ly dimin­ished either his finan­cial reck­less­ness or his obses­sion with ukiyo‑e. The mas­ters of that clas­si­cal “art of the float­ing world” like Hoku­sai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenag­er, Wright went to work for the archi­tect Joseph Sils­bee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle.
“Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenol­losa, hap­pened to be the world’s lead­ing West­ern expert on Japan­ese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Con­ver­sa­tion. It isn’t cer­tain how well the young Wright knew Fenol­losa — or indeed when he began col­lect­ing ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hoku­sai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Expo­si­tion in Chica­go in 1893, “about the time he opened his prac­tice in Oak Park.”

Eight years lat­er, “Wright made his first voy­age to Japan in pur­suit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough exper­tise to stage an exhi­bi­tion of his own Hiroshige col­lec­tion at the Art Insti­tute of Chica­go in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, mak­ing it clear that he was only inter­est­ed in using that time to acquire more prints. Lat­er, while work­ing on the Impe­r­i­al Hotel between 1917 and 1922, he spent a total of more than three years there, lat­er writ­ing that “the pur­suit of the Japan­ese print became my con­stant recre­ation while in Tokio,” a quest whose “adven­tures and excur­sions would take place at night or some­times call for a jour­ney by day to dis­tant places.” This posi­tioned him well to take on a side­line as a deal­er (or as he liked to call him­self, a mer­chant) of Japan­ese art in a Unit­ed States only just becom­ing aware of its beau­ty — an espe­cial­ly advan­ta­geous con­di­tion in archi­tec­tural­ly lean years.

Wright val­ued ukiyo‑e, about which he pub­lished a book in 1912, for its sense of order, struc­ture, nature, and sim­plic­i­ty. “Five lines where three are enough is stu­pid­i­ty,” he wrote. “Nine pounds where three are suf­fi­cient is stu­pid­i­ty. But to elim­i­nate expres­sive words that inten­si­fy or viv­i­fy mean­ing in speak­ing or writ­ing is not sim­plic­i­ty.” In his own form, he under­stood full well that “expres­sive changes of sur­face, empha­sis of line, and espe­cial­ly tex­tures of mate­r­i­al, may go to make facts elo­quent — forms more sig­nif­i­cant.” But it was Hoku­sai, Hiroshige, and count­less oth­er com­mer­cial artists of that ear­li­er time and dis­tant land that changed his approach to build­ing in the first place. “When I saw the print and I saw the elim­i­na­tion of the insignif­i­cant and sim­plic­i­ty of vision, togeth­er with the sense of rhythm and the impor­tance of design, I began to see nature in a total­ly dif­fer­ent way.” And thus, thanks to Japan­ese art, did that most Amer­i­can of all archi­tects begin tak­ing shape.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: How the Japanese Practice of “Forest Bathing”—Or Just Hanging Out in the Woods—Can Lower Stress Levels and Fight Disease
description: When the U.S. media began report­ing on the phe­nom­e­non of “for­est bathing” as a ther­a­py for men­tal and phys­i­cal health, the online c
body:
When the U.S. media began report­ing on the phe­nom­e­non of “for­est bathing” as a ther­a­py for men­tal and phys­i­cal health, the online commentariat—as it will—mocked the con­cept relent­less­ly as yet anoth­er pre­ten­tious, bour­geois repack­ag­ing of some­thing thor­ough­ly mun­dane. Didn’t we just used to call it “going out­side”?
Well, yes, if all “for­est bathing” means is “going out­side,” then it does sound like a grandiose and unnec­es­sary phrase. The term, how­ev­er, is not an Amer­i­can mar­ket­ing inven­tion but a trans­la­tion of the Japan­ese shin­rin-yoku. “Coined by the Japan­ese Min­istry of Agri­cul­ture, Forestry and Fish­eries in 1982,” writes Meeri Kim at The Wash­ing­ton Post, “the word lit­er­al­ly trans­lates to ‘tak­ing in the for­est atmos­phere’ or ‘for­est bathing’ and refers to the process of soak­ing up the sights, smells and sounds of a nat­ur­al set­ting to pro­mote phys­i­o­log­i­cal and psy­cho­log­i­cal health.”
So what? We already have the exam­ples of thou­sands of years of Bud­dhist monks (and Thich Nhat Hanh), of Hen­ry David Thore­au, and the saints of the Sier­ra Club. But the old­est and most use­ful ideas and prac­tices can get care­less­ly dis­card­ed in the fran­tic pur­suit of inno­va­tion at all costs. The push­ing of hi-tech out­door gear, wear­able activ­i­ty track­ers, and health apps that ask us to log every move­ment can make going out­side feel like a daunt­ing, expen­sive chore or a com­pet­i­tive event.
For­est bathing involves none of those things. “Just be with the trees,” as Ephrat Livni describes the prac­tice, “no hik­ing, no count­ing steps on a Fit­bit. You can sit or mean­der, but the point is to relax rather than accom­plish any­thing.” You don’t have to hug the trees if you don’t want to, but at least sit under one for a spell. Even if you don’t attain enlight­en­ment, you very well may reduce stress and boost immune func­tion, accord­ing to sev­er­al Japan­ese stud­ies con­duct­ed between 2004 and 2012.
The Japan­ese gov­ern­ment spent around four mil­lion dol­lars on stud­ies con­duct­ed with hun­dreds of peo­ple “bathing” on 48 des­ig­nat­ed ther­a­py trails. In his work, Qing Li, asso­ciate pro­fes­sor at Nip­pon Med­ical School in Tokyo, found “sig­nif­i­cant increas­es in NK [nat­ur­al killer] cell activ­i­ty in the week after a for­est vis­it… pos­i­tive effects last­ed a month fol­low­ing each week­end in the woods.” Nat­ur­al killer cells fight virus­es and can­cers, and are appar­ent­ly stim­u­lat­ed by the oils that trees them­selves secrete to ward off germs and pests. See the pro­fes­sor explain in the video above (he trans­lates shin­rin-yoku as tak­ing a “for­est show­er,” and also claims to have bot­tled some of the effects).
Addi­tion­al­ly, exper­i­ments con­duct­ed by Japan’s Chi­ba Uni­ver­si­ty found that for­est bathing low­ered heart rate and blood pres­sure and brought down lev­els of cor­ti­sol, the stress hor­mone that can wreak hav­oc on every sys­tem when large amounts cir­cu­late through the body. Then there are the less tan­gi­ble psy­cho­log­i­cal ben­e­fits of tak­ing in the trees. Sub­jects in one study “showed sig­nif­i­cant­ly reduced hos­til­i­ty and depres­sion scores” after a walk in the woods. These find­ings under­score that spend­ing time in the for­est is a med­ical inter­ven­tion as well as an aes­thet­ic and spir­i­tu­al one, some­thing sci­en­tists have long observed but haven’t been able to quan­ti­fy.
In their review of a book called Your Brain on Nature, Moth­er Earth News quotes Franklin Hough, first chief of the U.S. Divi­sion of Forestry, who remarked in a 19th cen­tu­ry med­ical jour­nal that forests have “a cheer­ful and tran­quil­iz­ing influ­ence which they exert upon the mind, more espe­cial­ly when worn down by men­tal labor.” Hough’s hypoth­e­sis has been con­firmed, and despite what might sound to Eng­lish speak­ers like a slight­ly ridicu­lous name, for­est bathing is seri­ous ther­a­py, espe­cial­ly for the ever-increas­ing num­ber of urban­ites and those who spend their days in strip malls, office com­plex­es, and oth­er over­built envi­ron­ments.
What is a guid­ed for­est bathing expe­ri­ence like? You can lis­ten to NPR’s Ali­son Aubrey describe one above. She quotes Amos Clif­ford, founder of the Asso­ci­a­tion of Nature & For­est Ther­a­py, the cer­ti­fy­ing orga­ni­za­tion, as say­ing that a guide “helps you be here, not there,” sort of like a med­i­ta­tion instruc­tor. Clif­ford has been push­ing health care providers to “incor­po­rate for­est ther­a­py as a stress-reduc­tion strat­e­gy” in the U.S., and there’s no ques­tion that more stress reduc­tion tools are sore­ly need­ed.
But, you may won­der, do you have to call it “for­est bathing,” or pay for a cer­ti­fied guide, join a group, and buy some fan­cy out­er­wear to get the ben­e­fits of hang­ing out with trees? I say, con­sid­er the words of John Muir, the inde­fati­ga­ble 19th cen­tu­ry nat­u­ral­ist, “father of the Nation­al Park Sys­tem,” and found­ing saint of the Sier­ra Club: In the eter­nal youth of Nature you may renew your own. Go qui­et­ly, alone; no harm will befall you. The quote may under­es­ti­mate the amount of risk or over­state the ben­e­fits, but you get the idea. Muir was not one to get tan­gled up in seman­tics or over­ly detailed analy­sis. Nonethe­less, his work inspired Amer­i­cans to step in and pre­serve so much of the coun­try’s for­est in the 19th and 20th cen­turies. Maybe the pre­ven­ta­tive med­i­cine of “for­est bathing” can help do the same in the 21st.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: 'The Otherworld Is Home' Explores Personal Reclamation, Cultural Identity, and Spiritual Passage
description: The Haggerty Museum of Art at Marquette University hosts free-to-the-public exhibitions and programs inviting a journey across multiple centuries
body:
The Haggerty Museum of Art at Marquette University hosts free-to-the-public exhibitions and programs inviting a journey across multiple centuries and continents titled The Otherworld is Home. Inspired by the Yorùbá proverb, “Life is a journey, the otherworld is home” (ayé l’àjò, ọ̀run n’ilé), the museum-wide presentation explores themes of personal reclamation, cultural identity, spiritual passage, and connection across Africa’s many diasporas.
The three simultaneous exhibitions below offer opportunities to explore the enduring resonance of African artistic traditions and their continued influence on contemporary life. These exhibitions are activated with a full slate of programming that may be found on the museum’s events page.

African Art: Ancient Roots, Enduring Values
Featuring more than 40 classical and neoclassical works, this exhibition highlights how African artists use traditional craftsmanship to connect the tangible and spiritual worlds. “This exhibition and essay explore how, what, and why African works of art . . . work: how they move and affect us; what roles they perform; and the ways they may acquire different purposes, meanings, and values as they travel across oceans and cultural, political, and religious boundaries over time and space,” writes guest curator and scholar of African and African diaspora arts Henry John Drewal.

Iké Udé: Sartorial Anarchy
Artist Iké Udé’s ongoing photographic series Sartorial Anarchy merges clothing and objects from different times and places to upend recognizable signifiers of cultural and individual identity. The Nigerian born artist, now living in New York City, transforms himself into a multifaceted amalgam of many identities in these photographic self-portraits. According to the artist, “In each image, I married disparate costumes from widely diverse traditions, countries, and time frames. And in mixing eras and cultures, I was able to bring harmony, as it were, to their similarly irreconcilable differences.”

Thresholds
Thresholds brings together the work of Aisha Tandiwe Bell, Portia Cobb, Stephen Hamilton, and Daniel Minter to dynamically explore the depth, complexity, and resilience of Black cultural memory. The artists create at a threshold between the seen and unseen, the present and the ancestral, and the place left behind and the place arrived at. Working across several media, they present their work alongside African works from the Haggerty’s collection to create a “call and response,” a participatory exchange in which one voice calls out and others answer in turn. Building on a shared yet continually unfolding cultural memory, where the past remains active and unresolved, these practices become sites of inspiration, critical reflection, and renewal.
To learn more, visit marquette.edu/haggerty-museum.

title: Henry Wessel's Candid California Photos Underscore the Art of Noticing
description: “There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) sa
body:
“There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) said in a “TateShots” short on the occasion of Tate Modern’s display of his Incidents series in 2014. Today, an exhibition of more than 65 prints titled Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books opens at The Grolier Club, a historic society celebrating the world of books and the graphic arts.
Wessel was a New Jersey native who, after borrowing a Leica camera during his studies at Pennsylvania State University, fell headlong into photography. He rose to prominence in the early 1970s for his black-and-white compositions that plumbed the possibilities of landscape and documentary imagery. Following the receipt of a Guggenheim grant, he moved to the Bay Area, where he taught at the now-defunct San Francisco Art Institute from 1973 to 2014 and captured the area’s characteristically glowing light, historic neighborhoods, and individualistic denizens.
“Untitled” (1968), gelatin silver print
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes the artist’s Incidents and Traffic series in their totality, plus works from his Real Estate and Night Walks series. To make the latter, he would walk around neighborhoods with his tripod and take portraits of local homes after dinner or during the early morning hours.
In Traffic, Wessel snapped scenes and other drivers from his car, capturing candid moments as other vehicles passed or as he encountered roadside curiosities. But he quickly learned that there’s an inherent issue with having to stop the car, get out, and try to capture what you initially saw: it looks totally different.
Wessel began to capture what he saw directly from the driver’s seat, working quickly with the hope that the images would more closely translate his immediate experiences. In an SFMOMA interview he said, “You know, like they say, luck is impartial. You have just as much bad luck as you have good luck. But you can do things to prepare yourself to receive the good luck. And that’s part of the whole process of photographing.”
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes some of Wessel’s earliest work, such as “Untitled” from 1968, plus the other series that were created throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The show opens today and continues through November 14 in New York, and a catalogue slated for release in October is available for pre-order from Chicago University Press.

title: Edge-to-Edge Splendor Fills Maria Yolanda Liebana's Buoyant Paintings
description: Tarot, pop culture, and personal narrative converge in the maximalist, mixed-media paintings of Maria Yolanda Liebana. The New York-based artist o
body:
Tarot, pop culture, and personal narrative converge in the maximalist, mixed-media paintings of Maria Yolanda Liebana. The New York-based artist opens her first institutional solo exhibition at Montclair State University’s George Segal Gallery this month.
Titled A Place to Be Held, Liebana’s show revolves around a fantastical, Eden-like garden exploding with an extravaganza of rainbows, flowers, clouds, cosmic phenomena, and more. “The exhibition imagines a matriarchal world where chance, identity, and desire are always in motion,” says a statement.
“The Aleph’s Seduction” (2024)
Liebana incorporates a wide range of materials into her vibrant works, including wallpaper, mirror tiles, pearls, glitter, disco balls, sequins, and rhinestones. She embraces the luminosity of joy and playfulness while nodding to Catholicism and ancient mythologies, invoked by symbols like chalices and cherubs.
As a first-generation Latinx immigrant who grew up in New Jersey, the artist has long been interested in the nature of selfhood and inheritance, and the birth of her daughter inspired a body of work that explores motherhood “as both a physical and spiritual terrain shaped by labor, wonder, and transformation.” She depicts confident, empowered women who dance, recline, and enjoy one another’s company, representing universal feminine dominion and strength.
A Place to Be Held opens on September 15 and continues through December 11 in Montclair, New Jersey. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Spanning 200+ Works, a New Book Celebrates the World of Fungi
description: Following surveys of butterflies, birds, oceans, and trees, the editors at Phaidon have settled on their next topic of inquiry: fungi. This Octobe
body:
Following surveys of butterflies, birds, oceans, and trees, the editors at Phaidon have settled on their next topic of inquiry: fungi. This October, the publisher will release an expansive tome gathering more than 200 photographs, artworks, historical objects, and more all devoted to the vast diversity and creative potential of mycology.
Fungi: The World of Mushrooms spans more than 200 pages and several millennia, compiling a breadth of imagery from ancient history to the present day. Included are the uncanny costumes shot in-situ by Riitta Ikonen and Anni Koponen, Hima af Klint’s delicate illustrations, and Carsten Höller’s disorienting installation of suspended toadstools.
Fungi is slated for release on October 15, and you can reserve your copy in the Colossal Shop.
